title: Python Programming Language
passage_text: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. Its design emphasizes code readability and simplicity.

title: World Wide Web Invention
passage_text: The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 while working at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland.

title: Linux Operating System
passage_text: Linux is a family of open-source Unix-like operating systems based on the Linux kernel, first released by Linus Torvalds in September 1991.

title: Transistor Invention
passage_text: The point-contact transistor was invented in December 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs.

title: Relational Database Management
passage_text: The relational model for database management was proposed by Edgar F. Codd in 1970 while working at IBM Research.

title: JavaScript Language
passage_text: JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich in 1995 while working at Netscape Communications Corporation.

title: TCP/IP Protocol
passage_text: The Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) suite was designed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the 1970s.

title: Quantum Computing Bits
passage_text: Quantum computers use qubits which can exist in superposition states, unlike classical bits which represent either 0 or 1.

title: Optical Fiber Communication
passage_text: Optical fibers transmit data as light pulses through strands of glass or plastic, enabling high-speed long-distance telecommunications.

title: Git Version Control
passage_text: Git is a distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for development of the Linux kernel.

title: C Programming Language
passage_text: The C programming language was developed by Dennis Ritchie between 1969 and 1973 at Bell Labs.

title: Artificial Neural Networks
passage_text: Artificial neural networks are computing systems inspired by biological neural networks that constitute animal brains.

title: Machine Learning Supervised
passage_text: Supervised learning algorithms build a mathematical model of a set of data that contains both inputs and desired outputs.

title: Flash Memory
passage_text: Flash memory is an electronic non-volatile computer storage medium invented by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba in the early 1980s.

title: Ethernet Networking
passage_text: Ethernet was developed at Xerox PARC by Robert Metcalfe and others in the early 1970s for local area networking.

title: Solid State Drives
passage_text: Solid-state drives use integrated circuit assemblies to store data persistently, typically using flash memory.

title: Bluetooth Technology
passage_text: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology standard managed by the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, introduced in 1998.

title: RISC-V Architecture
passage_text: RISC-V is an open standard instruction set architecture based on established reduced instruction set computer principles.

title: Graphics Processing Units
passage_text: GPUs are specialized electronic circuits designed to accelerate computer graphics processing and parallel workloads.

title: Public Key Cryptography
passage_text: Public-key cryptography was introduced publicly by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in their landmark 1976 paper.

title: Android Operating System
passage_text: Android was developed by Android Inc., which Google acquired in 2005, and is based on a modified version of the Linux kernel.

title: Speed of Light
passage_text: The speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, a fundamental physical constant.

title: DNA Double Helix
passage_text: The double helix structure of DNA was determined in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick, using X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin.

title: General Relativity
passage_text: Albert Einstein published the general theory of relativity in 1915, describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

title: Periodic Table
passage_text: Dmitri Mendeleev formulated the periodic law and published the first widely recognized periodic table in 1869.

title: Photosynthesis Process
passage_text: Photosynthesis is used by plants and other organisms to convert light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrate molecules.

title: Water Chemical Formula
passage_text: Water is a chemical compound consisting of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, denoted as H2O.

title: Hubble Space Telescope
passage_text: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into low Earth orbit in April 1990 aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery.

title: Electron Discovery
passage_text: The electron was discovered in 1897 by J. J. Thomson during experiments with cathode ray tubes.

title: Neutron Discovery
passage_text: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935.

title: Plate Tectonics Theory
passage_text: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory describing the large-scale motion of seven large plates and many smaller plates of Earth's lithosphere.

title: First Law of Thermodynamics
passage_text: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

title: Mitochondria Function
passage_text: Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles found in most eukaryotic organisms that generate most of the cell's ATP.

title: Big Bang Theory
passage_text: The Big Bang model suggests the universe expanded from an extremely high-density and high-temperature initial state roughly 13.8 billion years ago.

title: Bohr Atomic Model
passage_text: Niels Bohr proposed his atomic model in 1913, introducing quantized electron orbits around the atomic nucleus.

title: Cell Theory
passage_text: Cell theory states that all living organisms are composed of cells and that new cells arise from pre-existing cells.

title: Radioactivity Discovery
passage_text: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 while investigating phosphorescence in uranium salts.

title: CRISPR Gene Editing
passage_text: CRISPR-Cas9 is a technology that allows geneticists and medical researchers to edit parts of the genome by cutting DNA sequences.

title: Ozone Layer Function
passage_text: The ozone layer absorbs between 97 and 99 percent of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light in Earth's stratosphere.

title: Penicillin Antibiotic
passage_text: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when he noticed that a Penicillium mould inhibited bacterial growth.

title: Gravitational Waves
passage_text: Gravitational waves were directly detected for the first time on September 14, 2015 by the LIGO interferometers.

title: Higgs Boson
passage_text: The Higgs boson was discovered at the Large Hadron Collider at CERN in 2012, confirming the existence of the Higgs field.

title: Apollo 11 Moon Landing
passage_text: Apollo 11 was the first crewed mission to land on the Moon on July 20, 1969, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins.

title: French Revolution
passage_text: The French Revolution began in 1789 with the storming of the Bastille and led to the abolition of the French monarchy.

title: Magna Carta
passage_text: The Magna Carta was signed in June 1215 at Runnymede by King John of England, establishing that monarchial rule was subject to law.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
passage_text: The Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, symbolizing the collapse of Soviet-backed communist regimes in Eastern Europe.

title: Treaty of Versailles
passage_text: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919, officially ending World War I between Germany and the Allied Powers.

title: United Nations Founding
passage_text: The United Nations was founded on October 24, 1945 following the ratification of the UN Charter by the five permanent Security Council members.

title: Industrial Revolution
passage_text: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the mid-18th century, transitioning manufacturing from hand production to machines.

title: Emancipation Proclamation
passage_text: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, declaring all enslaved persons in Confederate states free.

title: Ancient Olympic Games
passage_text: The ancient Olympic Games originated in Olympia, Greece, with the first recorded games held in 776 BC.

title: Battle of Hastings
passage_text: The Battle of Hastings took place on October 14, 1066, resulting in the Norman conquest of England under William the Conqueror.

passage_text: The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 AD when the last Western Roman Emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer.

title: Suez Canal Opening
passage_text: The Suez Canal in Egypt officially opened on November 17, 1869, connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.

title: Renaissance Era
passage_text: The Renaissance was a cultural movement that began in Florence, Italy in the 14th century and spread throughout Europe.

title: American Declaration of Independence
passage_text: The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776.

title: Panama Canal Completion
passage_text: The Panama Canal was opened on August 15, 1914, connecting the Atlantic Ocean with the Pacific Ocean across the Isthmus of Panama.

title: World War II End
passage_text: World War II in Europe concluded with the surrender of Nazi Germany on May 8, 1945 (V-E Day).

title: Sputnik 1 Launch
passage_text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite, on October 4, 1957.

title: Printing Press Invention
passage_text: Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable-type printing to Europe around 1440, revolutionizing book manufacturing.

title: Silk Road Trade
passage_text: The Silk Road was an ancient network of Eurasian trade routes that connected East Asia with the Mediterranean from the Han dynasty onwards.

title: Discovery of Tutankhamun Tomb
passage_text: Howard Carter discovered the intact tomb of the 18th Dynasty Pharaoh Tutankhamun in November 1922 in the Valley of the Kings.

title: Mount Everest Altitude
passage_text: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, reaching 8,848.86 metres in the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and China.

title: Amazon River Length
passage_text: The Amazon River in South America is the largest river by discharge volume of water in the world and the second longest after the Nile.

title: Sahara Desert
passage_text: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering over 9 million square kilometres across North Africa.

title: Mariana Trench
passage_text: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, reaching approximately 10,994 metres.

title: Lake Baikal
passage_text: Lake Baikal in southern Russia is the world's deepest and oldest freshwater lake, containing about 20% of Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water.

title: Nile River
passage_text: The Nile River flows northward through northeastern Africa and is generally considered the longest river in the world at approximately 6,650 km.

title: Great Barrier Reef
passage_text: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system, located in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland, Australia.

title: Dead Sea Elevation
passage_text: The shores of the Dead Sea in the Jordan Rift Valley are the lowest land elevation on Earth, at roughly 430 metres below sea level.

title: Antarctica Ice Sheet
passage_text: The Antarctic ice sheet is the largest single mass of ice on Earth, covering an area of nearly 14 million square kilometres.

title: Greenland Landmass
passage_text: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent, situated between the Arctic and Atlantic Oceans.

title: Victoria Falls
passage_text: Victoria Falls is a waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa between Zambia and Zimbabwe, spanning roughly 1,708 metres in width.

title: Grand Canyon
passage_text: The Grand Canyon is a steep-sided canyon carved by the Colorado River in Arizona, United States, reaching up to 1,800 metres in depth.

title: Caspian Sea
passage_text: The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland body of water, categorized as either the largest lake or a full sea.

title: Mount Kilimanjaro
passage_text: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania is a dormant volcano and the highest single free-standing mountain peak in Africa at 5,895 metres.

title: Atacama Desert Aridity
passage_text: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is considered the driest non-polar desert in the world.

title: Bering Strait
passage_text: The Bering Strait connects the Arctic Ocean with the Bering Sea and separates the Asian and North American continents by about 82 km.

title: K2 Mountain
passage_text: K2 is the second-highest mountain on Earth at 8,611 metres, located on the China-Pakistan border in the Karakoram range.

title: Suez Isthmus
passage_text: The Isthmus of Suez is the narrow strip of land that connects the continents of Africa and Asia.

title: Yellowstone Caldera
passage_text: The Yellowstone Caldera in Wyoming is a supervolcano volcanic caldera formed during three supereruptions over the past 2.1 million years.

title: Angel Falls
passage_text: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, with a height of 979 metres and a plunge of 807 metres.

title: Bicameral Legislature
passage_text: A bicameral legislature is a legislative body consisting of two separate houses or chambers, such as the US Senate and House of Representatives.

title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
passage_text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on December 10, 1948.

title: US Constitution Ratification
passage_text: The Constitution of the United States was drafted in 1787 and ratified in 1788, establishing the framework of the federal government.

title: European Union Parliament
passage_text: The European Parliament is the directly elected parliamentary institution of the European Union, representing EU citizens.

title: Geneva Conventions
passage_text: The Geneva Conventions are four treaties and three protocols establishing international legal standards for humanitarian treatment during war.

title: Constitutional Monarchy
passage_text: A constitutional monarchy is a form of monarchy in which the monarch exercises authority in accordance with a constitution.

title: Supreme Court of the US
passage_text: The Supreme Court of the United States consists of the Chief Justice and eight associate justices appointed for life under good behavior.

title: International Court of Justice
passage_text: The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, seated in The Hague, Netherlands.

title: Parliamentary Republic
passage_text: In a parliamentary republic, the executive branch derives its democratic legitimacy from and is accountable to the legislature.

title: Electoral College
passage_text: The United States Electoral College is the group of presidential electors formed every four years to elect the president and vice president.

title: Separation of Powers
passage_text: The doctrine of separation of powers divides governance into three independent branches: legislative, executive, and judicial.

title: NATO Alliance
passage_text: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is an intergovernmental military alliance between 32 member states from Europe and North America.

title: Cabinet Government
passage_text: A cabinet is a body of high-ranking state officials, typically consisting of top leaders of the executive branch.

title: Treaty of Rome
passage_text: The Treaty of Rome was signed on March 25, 1957, establishing the European Economic Community (EEC).

title: Veto Power UN Security Council
passage_text: The five permanent members of the UN Security Council (China, France, Russia, UK, US) hold veto power over substantive resolutions.

title: Magna Carta Rule of Law
passage_text: The Magna Carta asserted the principle of the rule of law, requiring the sovereign to be bound by legal constraints.

title: Federalism Concept
passage_text: Federalism is a system of government where power is divided between a central national authority and constituent political units.

title: Direct Democracy
passage_text: Direct democracy is a form of democracy in which citizens decide on policy initiatives directly rather than electing representatives.

title: Universal Suffrage
passage_text: Universal suffrage grants the right to vote to all adult citizens regardless of wealth, income, gender, or social status.

title: Judicial Review
passage_text: Judicial review is the power of a court to review statutory enactments and executive acts to determine constitutional validity.

title: Central Bank Monetary Policy
passage_text: Central banks use monetary-policy tools, including interest rates and reserve requirements, to regulate money supply and inflation.

title: Gross Domestic Product
passage_text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a monetary measure of the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country over a specific time period.

title: Inflation Definition
passage_text: Inflation is the general rise in the price level of goods and services in an economy over a sustained period.

title: Bretton Woods Conference
passage_text: The Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944 established the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

title: Law of Supply and Demand
passage_text: The law of supply and demand describes how the price of an asset or commodity is determined by the balance of availability and consumer desire.

title: World Bank Mission
passage_text: The World Bank is an international financial institution that provides loans and grants to low- and middle-income countries for capital projects.

title: Fiscal Policy
passage_text: Fiscal policy refers to government spending and taxation decisions used to influence macroeconomic conditions.

title: Comparative Advantage
passage_text: The theory of comparative advantage, formulated by David Ricardo, shows how countries benefit from trade by specializing in goods they produce with lower opportunity costs.

title: Federal Reserve System
passage_text: The Federal Reserve is the central banking system of the United States, created on December 23, 1913 by the Federal Reserve Act.

title: Opportunity Cost
passage_text: Opportunity cost represents the potential benefits an individual, investor, or business misses out on when choosing one alternative over another.

title: Purchasing Power Parity
passage_text: Purchasing power parity is an economic metric comparing economic productivity and standards of living between countries.

title: Keynesian Economics
passage_text: Keynesian economics is a macroeconomic theory developed by John Maynard Keynes advocating government intervention during economic downturns.

title: Stock Market Index
passage_text: A stock market index measures a hypothetical portfolio of investment holdings to indicate performance of a market sector or economy.

title: Tariff Definition
passage_text: A tariff is a customs duty or tax levied on imports of goods and services by a sovereign government.

title: Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics
passage_text: Microeconomics analyzes individual agents and markets, while macroeconomics studies aggregated economy-wide phenomena such as unemployment and GDP.

title: Monopoly Market Structure
passage_text: A monopoly exists when a single enterprise is the only supplier of a particular commodity or service in a given market.

title: Elasticity of Demand
passage_text: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.

title: Balance of Payments
passage_text: The balance of payments records all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a specified period.

title: Cryptocurrency Decentralization
passage_text: Cryptocurrencies use decentralized consensus mechanisms on distributed ledgers to verify transactions without requiring central clearing houses.

title: Gini Coefficient
passage_text: The Gini coefficient is a statistical measure of economic inequality across a population, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

title: Olympic Games Modern
passage_text: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece in April 1896, organized by the International Olympic Committee.

title: FIFA World Cup 1930
passage_text: The inaugural FIFA World Cup took place in Uruguay in July 1930, with Uruguay winning the championship match.

title: Marathon Distance
passage_text: The standard marathon distance is 42.195 kilometres (26 miles 385 yards), established officially at the 1908 London Olympic Games.

title: Tour de France
passage_text: The Tour de France is an annual men's multiple-stage bicycle race primarily held in France, first organized in 1903 by Géo Lefèvre.

title: Basketball Invention
passage_text: James Naismith invented the game of basketball in December 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, writing the original 13 rules.

title: Wimbledon Championship
passage_text: The Championships, Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world, founded in 1877 at the All England Club in London.

title: Super Bowl History
passage_text: The first AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later known as Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967 in Los Angeles.

title: Cricket Laws
passage_text: The Laws of Cricket were first drawn up in 1744 and are maintained and copyrighted by the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) in London.

title: Summer Olympics Frequency
passage_text: The Summer Olympic Games are held every four years, with the exception of cancellations during World Wars I and II and the 2020 postponement.

title: World Athletics Record 100m
passage_text: Usain Bolt of Jamaica set the world record in the 100 metres sprint at 9.58 seconds in Berlin on August 16, 2009.

title: Formula One Championship
passage_text: The Formula One World Championship was founded in 1950, with the first race held at the Silverstone Circuit in England.

title: Rugby World Cup
passage_text: The inaugural Rugby World Cup took place in 1987, co-hosted by New Zealand and Australia, with New Zealand winning the title.

title: Ryder Cup
passage_text: The Ryder Cup is a biennial men's golf competition between teams from Europe and the United States, initiated in 1927.

title: Paralympic Games
passage_text: The first official Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960, bringing together 400 athletes from 23 countries.

title: Volleyball Invention
passage_text: William G. Morgan invented volleyball in Holyoke, Massachusetts in 1895, originally naming the sport Mintonette.

title: Decathlon Events
passage_text: The Olympic decathlon consists of ten track and field events held over two consecutive days.

title: Baseball World Series
passage_text: The World Series is the annual championship series of Major League Baseball, first played in 1903 between Boston and Pittsburgh.

title: Stanley Cup
passage_text: The Stanley Cup is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America, commissioned in 1892.

title: Badminton Scoring
passage_text: In international badminton, a match consists of the best of three games of 21 points using rally scoring.

title: PGA Tour
passage_text: The PGA Tour is the organizer of the main professional golf tours played by men in the United States and North America.

title: Penicillin Discovery Fleming
passage_text: Penicillin was discovered in September 1928 by Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital in London, revolutionizing antibacterial treatment.

title: Smallpox Eradication
passage_text: Smallpox was officially declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in May 1980 following a global vaccination campaign.

title: Insulin Discovery
passage_text: Insulin was discovered in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best working in the laboratory of J. J. R. Macleod at the University of Toronto.

title: Polio Vaccine Salk
passage_text: Jonas Salk developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, announced as safe and effective on April 12, 1955.

title: World Health Organization Function
passage_text: The World Health Organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health.

title: Human Genome Project
passage_text: The Human Genome Project was an international research project completed in April 2003 that sequenced the vast majority of human DNA base pairs.

title: Antibiotic Resistance
passage_text: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria adapt and survive exposure to antibiotics designed to inhibit or kill them.

title: Cardiovascular System
passage_text: The cardiovascular system consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood, functioning to transport oxygen and nutrients to tissues throughout the body.

title: Tuberculosis Causative Agent
passage_text: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, identified by Robert Koch in 1882.

title: Hemoglobin Function
passage_text: Hemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the respiratory organs to the rest of the body.

title: Immune System T Cells
passage_text: T lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell of the immune system that mature in the thymus gland and participate in cell-mediated immunity.

title: Aspirin History
passage_text: Felix Hoffmann synthesized acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in 1897 at the Bayer company in Germany.

title: Diabetes Types
passage_text: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin, whereas Type 2 involves insulin resistance.

title: Blood Pressure Measurement
passage_text: Blood pressure is recorded as systolic pressure over diastolic pressure, measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).

title: DNA Structure Discovery
passage_text: James Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins were awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for nucleic acid structural discoveries.

title: Vaccination Principle
passage_text: Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens by exposing it to an antigen derived from the microbe.

title: X-Ray Discovery
passage_text: Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen discovered X-rays in 1895, receiving the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for this breakthrough.

title: Malaria Parasite
passage_text: Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by parasitic protozoans of the genus Plasmodium.

title: Clinical Trial Phases
passage_text: Clinical drug development proceeds through Phase I (safety), Phase II (efficacy/dosing), Phase III (large-scale confirmation), and Phase IV (post-marketing).

title: Hippocratic Oath
passage_text: The Hippocratic Oath is an oath of ethics historically taken by physicians, traditionally attributed to Hippocrates of Kos.

title: Paris Climate Agreement
passage_text: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by 196 parties at COP 21 in Paris on December 12, 2015.

title: Greenhouse Effect
passage_text: The greenhouse effect is the process by which radiation from a planet's atmosphere warms the planet's surface to a temperature above what it would be without its atmosphere.

title: Carbon Cycle
passage_text: The carbon cycle is the biogeochemical cycle by which carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, pedosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere of Earth.

title: Deforestation Impact
passage_text: Deforestation contributes to habitat loss, decreased biodiversity, and the release of sequestered carbon into the atmosphere.

title: Renewable Energy Sources
passage_text: Renewable energy comes from natural sources that are constantly replenished, including solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, and biomass energy.

title: Biodiversity Hotspots
passage_text: A biodiversity hotspot is a biogeographic region with significant levels of biodiversity that is threatened by human habitation.

title: Ocean Acidification
passage_text: Ocean acidification is the ongoing decrease in the pH of Earth's oceans caused by the uptake of anthropogenic carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

title: Kyoto Protocol
passage_text: The Kyoto Protocol was an international treaty adopted on December 11, 1997, committing industrialized countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
passage_text: The IPCC was created in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme to provide scientific assessments on climate change.

title: Wetlands Ecological Role
passage_text: Wetlands act as natural water filters, mitigate flood risks, and provide critical habitats for migratory birds and aquatic species.

title: Plastic Pollution in Oceans
passage_text: Plastic waste in marine environments breaks down into microplastics, which enter the marine food web and cause broad ecological damage.

title: Endangered Species Act
passage_text: The United States Endangered Species Act of 1973 provides a framework to conserve and protect endangered and threatened species and their habitats.

title: Tundra Ecosystem
passage_text: Tundra is a biome where tree growth is hindered by low temperatures and short growing seasons, characterized by permafrost soils.

title: Amazon Rainforest Carbon Sink
passage_text: The Amazon basin contains the largest tropical rainforest in the world and stores an estimated 150-200 billion tonnes of carbon.

title: Montréal Protocol
passage_text: The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was agreed in 1987, successfully phasing out the production of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

title: Eutrophication Process
passage_text: Eutrophication occurs when a water body becomes overly enriched with nutrients, leading to excessive algae growth and hypoxia.

title: Coral Bleaching Causes
passage_text: Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel symbiotic zooxanthellae algae due to elevated water temperatures or pollution.

title: Ramsar Convention
passage_text: The Ramsar Convention is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, signed in Ramsar, Iran in 1971.

title: Soil Degradation
passage_text: Soil erosion and nutrient depletion reduce agricultural productivity and undermine terrestrial ecosystem stability worldwide.

title: Species Extinction Rates
passage_text: Current species extinction rates are estimated by conservation biologists to be 100 to 1,000 times higher than the natural background rate.

title: Formative Assessment
passage_text: Formative assessment takes place during instruction and is intended to provide feedback that can guide teaching and improve learning.

title: Summative Assessment
passage_text: Summative assessment evaluates student learning at the end of an instructional unit by comparing it against some standard or benchmark.

title: Bloom's Taxonomy
passage_text: Bloom's Taxonomy, published in 1956 by Benjamin Bloom and collaborators, classifies educational learning objectives into cognitive complexity levels.

title: Montessori Education
passage_text: Montessori education is a child-centered educational approach developed by Italian physician Maria Montessori in the early 20th century.

title: Pedagogy Definition
passage_text: Pedagogy is the method and practice of teaching, especially as an academic subject or theoretical concept.

title: Higher Education Bologna Process
passage_text: The Bologna Process is a series of agreements between European countries to ensure comparability in the standards and quality of higher-education qualifications.

title: Vygotsky Scaffolding
passage_text: Lev Vygotsky introduced the concept of the Zone of Proximal Development, describing what a learner can do with guidance versus independently.

title: Peer Assessment
passage_text: Peer assessment involves students evaluating the work of their peers based on predefined criteria and performance standards.

title: University of Bologna
passage_text: The University of Bologna in Italy, founded in 1088, is widely considered the oldest continuously operating university in the world.

title: Inclusive Education
passage_text: Inclusive education ensures that students with diverse learning needs and disabilities are educated in general classroom environments alongside their peers.

title: STEM Education
passage_text: STEM education integrates science, technology, engineering, and mathematics into an interdisciplinary and applied curriculum.

title: PISA International Assessment
passage_text: The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is a worldwide study by the OECD measuring 15-year-old school pupils' scholastic performance.

title: Jean Piaget Stages of Development
passage_text: Jean Piaget proposed four stages of cognitive development: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational.

title: Distance Learning Evolution
passage_text: Distance education has evolved from correspondence courses using postal mail to modern synchronous and asynchronous digital e-learning platforms.

title: Curriculum Development
passage_text: Curriculum design involves organizing learning goals, instructional activities, and evaluation methods into a coherent instructional sequence.

title: Adult Learning Theory Andragogy
passage_text: Malcolm Knowles popularized andragogy, arguing that adults learn differently from children due to self-directedness and accumulated life experience.

title: Standardized Testing
passage_text: Standardized tests require all test takers to answer the same questions in the same way, scored in a consistent manner to compare relative performance.

title: Oxford University
passage_text: The University of Oxford in England has evidence of teaching as early as 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world.

title: Gamification in Learning
passage_text: Educational gamification incorporates game design elements into non-game learning environments to enhance engagement and motivation.

title: Open Educational Resources
passage_text: Open Educational Resources are teaching and research materials in the public domain or released under an open license permitting free reuse.

title: Mars Satellites Phobos Deimos
passage_text: Mars has two small natural satellites, Phobos and Deimos, discovered by Asaph Hall in August 1877.

title: Jupiter Great Red Spot
passage_text: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a persistent high-pressure storm in the planet's atmosphere, observed continuously since at least 1878.

title: Saturn Ring System
passage_text: Saturn's planetary ring system is the most extensive in the Solar System, composed predominantly of water ice particles with trace rock debris.

title: James Webb Space Telescope
passage_text: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on December 25, 2021, operating near the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point to observe infrared astronomy.

title: International Space Station
passage_text: The International Space Station is a modular space station in low Earth orbit, continuously occupied by international crews since November 2000.

title: Voyager 1 Interstellar Mission
passage_text: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched in September 1977, entered interstellar space in August 2012, becoming the most distant human-made object.

title: Pluto Reclassification
passage_text: The International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto from a planet to a dwarf planet in August 2006.

title: Solar System Planets Count
passage_text: The Solar System contains eight recognized planets orbiting the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

title: Hubble Deep Field
passage_text: The Hubble Deep Field image, captured in 1995, revealed thousands of galaxies in a tiny region of space previously thought to be mostly empty.

title: Venus Atmosphere
passage_text: Venus has an extremely dense atmosphere composed mainly of carbon dioxide with clouds of sulfuric acid, creating a runaway greenhouse effect.

title: Exoplanet Detection Kepler
passage_text: NASA's Kepler space telescope discovered thousands of confirmed exoplanets using the transit photometry method between 2009 and 2018.

title: Supermassive Black Hole Sagittarius A*
passage_text: Sagittarius A* is a supermassive black hole at the Galactic Center of the Milky Way, with a mass of roughly 4 million solar masses.

title: Lunar Phases Mechanism
passage_text: Lunar phases result from the changing geometry between the Sun, Earth, and Moon as the Moon orbits Earth roughly every 29.5 days.

title: Kuiper Belt
passage_text: The Kuiper Belt is a circumstellar disc in the outer Solar System extending beyond Neptune's orbit, containing icy bodies and dwarf planets.

title: Apollo 17 Mission
passage_text: Apollo 17 was the final mission of NASA's Apollo program, landing Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt on the Moon in December 1972.

title: Comet Halley Orbit
passage_text: Halley's Comet is a periodic comet with an orbital period of approximately 75 to 76 years, last seen in the inner Solar System in 1986.

title: Mars Curiosity Rover
passage_text: NASA's Curiosity rover landed in Gale Crater on Mars in August 2012 to investigate past Martian habitability and geology.

title: Solar Flares
passage_text: Solar flares are intense localized eruptions of electromagnetic radiation in the Sun's atmosphere caused by magnetic field reconnection.

title: Oort Cloud
passage_text: The Oort cloud is a theoretical cloud of predominantly icy planetesimals proposed to surround the Sun at distances up to 100,000 AU.

title: Titan Moon of Saturn
passage_text: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only known moon with a dense atmosphere and stable surface liquid hydrocarbon lakes.

title: World Health Organization Structure
passage_text: The World Health Organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health, founded in 1948.

title: Apple Inc Founding
passage_text: Apple Inc. was founded on April 1, 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne to develop and sell the Apple I personal computer.

title: Microsoft Founding
passage_text: Microsoft was founded on April 4, 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen to develop and sell BASIC interpreters for the Altair 8800.

title: Google Founding
passage_text: Google was founded on September 4, 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin while they were PhD students at Stanford University.

title: Amazon Founding
passage_text: Amazon was founded on July 5, 1994 by Jeff Bezos in Bellevue, Washington, starting as an online marketplace for books.

title: International Monetary Fund
passage_text: The IMF is an international financial organization of 190 member countries working to foster global monetary cooperation and financial stability.

title: Red Cross Movement
passage_text: The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement was founded in 1863 in Geneva, Switzerland by Henry Dunant.

title: CERN Laboratory
passage_text: CERN is the European Organization for Nuclear Research, operating the largest particle physics laboratory in the world near Geneva.

title: UNESCO Organization
passage_text: UNESCO is a specialized agency of the United Nations aimed at promoting world peace and security through international cooperation in education and science.

title: Toyota Motor Corporation
passage_text: Toyota Motor Corporation was founded on August 28, 1937 by Kiichiro Toyoda as a spinoff from his father's company Toyoda Automatic Loom Works.

title: IBM History
passage_text: IBM was founded on June 16, 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company (CTR) and renamed International Business Machines in 1924.

title: World Trade Organization
passage_text: The World Trade Organization was established on January 1, 1995 under the 1994 Marrakesh Agreement, replacing the GATT.

title: SpaceX Founding
passage_text: SpaceX was founded in March 2002 by Elon Musk with the goal of reducing space transportation costs to enable the colonization of Mars.

title: Amnesty International
passage_text: Amnesty International was founded in London in July 1961 by lawyer Peter Benenson to campaign for human rights globally.

title: Sony Corporation
passage_text: Sony was established on May 7, 1946 by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita in Tokyo, Japan, originally under the name Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo.

title: Doctors Without Borders
passage_text: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) was founded in 1971 by French doctors and journalists following the Nigerian Civil War.

title: OpenAI Founding
passage_text: OpenAI was founded in December 2015 as a non-profit artificial intelligence research organization in San Francisco, California.

title: Boeing Company
passage_text: The Boeing Company was founded by William Boeing in Seattle, Washington on July 15, 1916, becoming a major aerospace manufacturer.

title: World Wildlife Fund
passage_text: WWF was founded on April 29, 1961 in Morges, Switzerland, working in the field of wilderness preservation and endangered species.

title: Intel Corporation
passage_text: Intel was founded on July 18, 1968 by semiconductor pioneers Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore in Mountain View, California.

title: William Shakespeare Hamlet
passage_text: William Shakespeare was an English playwright and poet who wrote tragedies including Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, and Macbeth.

title: Albert Einstein Nobel Prize
passage_text: Albert Einstein was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

title: Marie Curie Nobel Prizes
passage_text: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields: Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

title: Isaac Newton Principia
passage_text: Sir Isaac Newton published Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica in 1687, formulating the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

title: Leonardo da Vinci Mona Lisa
passage_text: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the Renaissance who painted masterpieces including the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

title: Nelson Mandela Presidency
passage_text: Nelson Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who served as President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999.

title: Charles Darwin Origin of Species
passage_text: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, introducing the scientific theory of evolution by natural selection.

title: Ada Lovelace Computer Program
passage_text: Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm intended to be carried out by Charles Babbage's mechanical Analytical Engine in 1843.

title: Mahatma Gandhi Nonviolence
passage_text: Mahatma Gandhi led the campaign for Indian independence through nonviolent civil disobedience, inspiring movements for civil rights worldwide.

title: Galileo Galilei Telescopic Observations
passage_text: Galileo Galilei made groundbreaking astronomical observations with his telescope in 1609-1610, discovering four largest moons of Jupiter.

title: Alan Turing Computing Legacy
passage_text: Alan Turing played a pivotal role in cracking intercepted coded messages at Bletchley Park and is considered the father of theoretical computer science.

title: Frida Kahlo Art
passage_text: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for her many self-portraits and works inspired by the nature and artifacts of Mexico.

title: Ludwig van Beethoven Symphonies
passage_text: Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer who composed nine symphonies, creating landmark works during the transition between the Classical and Romantic eras.

title: Nikola Tesla Alternating Current
passage_text: Nikola Tesla contributed significantly to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system.

title: Jane Goodall Primatology
passage_text: Jane Goodall is an English primatologist and anthropologist renowned for her landmark 60-year study of chimpanzee social interactions in Gombe Stream National Park.

title: Winston Churchill Leadership
passage_text: Winston Churchill served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 during the Second World War.

title: Ernest Hemingway Literature
passage_text: Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist and short-story writer who received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.

title: Aristotle Philosophy
passage_text: Aristotle was an Ancient Greek philosopher whose writings covered physics, biology, zoology, metaphysics, ethics, and poetry.

title: Martin Luther King Jr Speech
passage_text: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech on August 28, 1963 during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

title: Steve Jobs Apple Leadership
passage_text: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple Inc. and later oversaw the creation of revolutionary products including the iMac, iPod, iPhone, and iPad.

title: Haiku Poetic Form
passage_text: Haiku is a traditional Japanese poetic form consisting of three phrases with a 5, 7, 5 syllable structure, often focusing on nature.

title: Renaissance Art Characteristics
passage_text: Renaissance art originated in Italy and is characterized by naturalism, mathematical perspective, and classical themes.

title: Gothic Architecture
passage_text: Gothic architecture originated in 12th-century France, distinguished by pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses.

title: Symphony Orchestra Structure
passage_text: A symphony orchestra is a large ensemble of musicians consisting of four instrumental families: strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.

title: Origami Paper Folding
passage_text: Origami is the traditional Japanese art of paper folding, creating intricate representations without using scissors or glue.

title: Kabuki Theatre
passage_text: Kabuki is a classical Japanese dance-drama known for its stylized performance, elaborate costumes, and distinctive kumadori makeup.

title: Tango Dance Origin
passage_text: Tango is a partner dance and musical genre that originated in the late 19th century in the border areas between Argentina and Uruguay.

title: Sonnet Poetic Structure
passage_text: A traditional Petrarchan or Shakespearean sonnet consists of 14 lines written in iambic pentameter with a specific rhyming scheme.

title: Impressionist Painting
passage_text: Impressionism was a 19th-century art movement in France characterized by visible brush strokes, open composition, and emphasis on accurate depiction of light.

title: Flamenco Music and Dance
passage_text: Flamenco is an art form based on the varied folkloric music traditions of southern Spain in the autonomous community of Andalusia.

title: Jazz Music Origins
passage_text: Jazz originated in the African-American communities of New Orleans in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, rooted in blues and ragtime.

title: Baroque Architecture
passage_text: Baroque architecture is a highly decorative style that originated in late 16th-century Italy, characterized by dynamic forms and dramatic lighting.

title: UNESCO World Heritage Sites
passage_text: UNESCO designates World Heritage Sites of outstanding cultural or natural importance to the common heritage of humanity.

title: Calligraphy Art
passage_text: Calligraphy is a visual art related to writing, designing and executing lettering with broad-tipped instruments or brushes.

title: Opera Art Form
passage_text: Opera is an art form in which singers and musicians perform a dramatic work combining text (libretto) and musical score in a theatrical setting.

title: Culinary Heritage UNESCO
passage_text: UNESCO recognizes traditional gastronomic cultures, including the Mediterranean diet and French gastronomic meal, as Intangible Cultural Heritage.

title: Carnival Celebrations
passage_text: Carnival is a Western Christian festive season occurring before Lent, celebrated with parades and masquerade balls, notably in Rio de Janeiro and Venice.

title: Surrealism Movement
passage_text: Surrealism was a 20th-century avant-garde movement in art and literature that sought to release the creative potential of the unconscious mind.

title: Cinema Lumiere Brothers
passage_text: Auguste and Louis Lumiere patented the Cinematographe in 1895 and presented the first commercial public screening of projected motion pictures in Paris.

title: Ballet Classical Dance
passage_text: Classical ballet is a formalized type of dance originating during the Italian Renaissance in the 15th century and developing into concert dance in France and Russia.

title: Water Freezing and Boiling Points
passage_text: Under standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm), pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius.

title: Earth Rotation Period
passage_text: Earth rotates once on its axis relative to distant stars in approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds (one sidereal day).

title: Leap Year Rule
passage_text: In the Gregorian calendar, a leap year occurs every four years, except for years divisible by 100 that are not also divisible by 400.

title: Alphabet Letters Count English
passage_text: The modern English alphabet contains 26 letters, consisting of five vowels (A, E, I, O, U) and 21 consonants.

title: Continents Number
passage_text: In the conventional seven-continent model, Earth's continents are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia.

title: Prime Number Definition
passage_text: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that cannot be formed by multiplying two smaller natural numbers.

title: Solar Eclipse Alignment
passage_text: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, thereby fully or partially obscuring the view of the Sun from Earth.

title: Atmospheric Composition
passage_text: Earth's atmosphere by dry volume consists of approximately 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, and trace other gases.

title: International Date Line
passage_text: The International Date Line is an internationally recognized calendar line on Earth's surface roughly following the 180th meridian of longitude.

title: Metric System SI Units
passage_text: The International System of Units (SI) defines seven fundamental base units: second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela.

title: Earth Moon Distance
passage_text: The average distance from the center of Earth to the center of the Moon is approximately 384,400 kilometres.

title: Human Chromosome Count
passage_text: Typical human cells contain 46 chromosomes organized into 23 homologous pairs, including two sex chromosomes.

title: Diamond Hardness Mohs
passage_text: Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring substance known, rating 10 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness.

title: Sound Speed in Air
passage_text: The speed of sound in dry air at 20 degrees Celsius is approximately 343 metres per second (1,235 km/h).

title: Primary Colors of Light
passage_text: In additive color mixing (such as on screens), the primary colors are red, green, and blue (RGB).

title: Richter Magnitude Scale
passage_text: The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale developed in 1935 by Charles F. Richter to quantify the energy released by earthquakes.

title: Rainbow Optical Phenomenon
passage_text: A rainbow is a meteorological optical phenomenon caused by reflection, refraction, and dispersion of light in water droplets.

title: Gold Chemical Element
passage_text: Gold is a chemical element with symbol Au and atomic number 79, known for its corrosion resistance and high electrical conductivity.

title: Compass Magnetic North
passage_text: A magnetic compass points towards the Earth's magnetic north pole, which differs slightly from the geographic North Pole.

title: Photosynthesis Oxygen Generation
passage_text: During photosynthesis, plants utilize water and carbon dioxide in the presence of sunlight to produce glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct.

title: Sunrise in the East
passage_text: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

title: Earth Orbit Around the Sun
passage_text: The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit, completing one revolution in approximately 365.25 days.

title: Water Boiling and Freezing
passage_text: Under standard atmospheric pressure, pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius and freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.

title: Speed of Light in Vacuum
passage_text: The speed of light in a vacuum is a universal constant equal to exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.

title: Earth Surface Gravity
passage_text: Standard gravity at Earth's surface accelerates freely falling objects downward at approximately 9.8 metres per second squared.

title: Atmospheric Composition
passage_text: Earth's atmosphere is composed of approximately 78 percent nitrogen gas and 21 percent oxygen, with trace amounts of argon and carbon dioxide.
